title: Tunisia: Authorities escalate assault on human rights with five-year prison sentence for Sihem Ben Sedrine
content:
Responding to the sentencing of prominent human rights defender and former Truth and Dignity Commission (IVD) president Sihem Ben Sedrine to five years in prison, Heba Morayef, Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa at Amnesty International, said today:

“This new sentence compounds the outrageous injustice against Sihem Ben Sedrine, who is being punished for her historic work as head of the transitional justice commission to expose decades of state abuses and for her years of steadfast human rights work.

“Sihem Ben Sedrine has already been sentenced to 25 years in prison following an unfair trial on bogus charges in two cases linked to her leadership of the Truth and Dignity Commission. While she has so far remained free pending her appeal, she faces an imminent risk of imprisonment.

title: Historic UN ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya is rare victory for survivors
content:
Responding to the ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ top court, that Myanmar authorities committed the crime of genocide in their clearance operations against Rohingya people in 2017, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnes Callamard said:

“Genocide. This is the unequivocal finding of the ICJ. After years of denial, impunity and suppression of truth, this ruling is a historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families.

“For decades, Myanmar governments and military authorities have denied the Rohingya citizenship and subjected them to an institutionalized system of segregation, discrimination and persecution that amounts to the crime against humanity of apartheid. They have confined Rohingya to refugee camps, burned their homes and villages, and committed widespread unlawful killings and sexual violence, including during the horrors of the military’s 2017 campaign.

title: Haiti: Kenscoff violence highlights continued risk of killing, abduction and other abuses against children by gangs – new research
content:
Children in Haiti remain at risk of killings, abductions, sexual violence and other abuses by armed gangs, Amnesty International said in new research ahead of World Children’s Day.

Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a municipal official. The UN said at least three boys and two girls were among those killed. A further 67 people, including 13 children, were abducted, according to municipal data.

Witnesses told Amnesty International that the attack began when dozens of gang members raided various parts of the commune of Kenscoff, south of Port-au-Prince. They attacked people in their homes, shooting them and setting houses on fire. They looted belongings and shot residents as they tried to escape. They also attacked displaced people who were taking shelter in the Ark of the New Covenant Church and shot many of them.

Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors

Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme

title: “Young people can question those in power and demand something better”
content:
Children and young people around the world continue to speak up despite challenges because they believe their actions can make a difference. Many of them are tackling the impact of climate change head on, some are struggling to get an education, while others face dangers when they protest.

The Spark Club is a group of 11 to 18-year-old activists from around the world working with Amnesty International to make sure their voices are included, heard and listened to. They have been instrumental in shaping Amnesty’s new briefing Sparking Change - Children’s Right to Protest: A Perspective from Children and Young Activists, working alongside our researchers.

Here three young activists share more about the challenges they face in their countries and how they’re holding their governments to account.  

I first understood how powerful social protest can be as I held my mother’s hand during a demonstration when I was very little. I learned not to stay quiet facing an injustice. 

Now I study Political Science in Buenos Aires University (UBA) and I focus my activism on fighting for human rights.

title: Global: Protesting children and young people face human rights abuses, including violence and discrimination
content:
Children and young people around the world face barriers, challenges and human rights abuses while exercising their right to protest, a new briefing from Amnesty International reveals, ahead of World Children’s Day on 20 November.

Sparking Change – Children’s Right to Protest: A Perspective from Children and Young Activists, is a briefing from Amnesty International developed in partnership with the Spark Club, a group of 11- to 17-year-olds from 12 countries across five regions. Drawing on research with more than 500 children and young people worldwide, the briefing examines why children protest, the risks they encounter, and what states and other actors must do to ensure that children can safely exercise their rights.

From the Gen-Z protests in Kenya to the Fridays for Future climate movement and recent youth-led demonstrations across Europe, young people have taken to the streets to make their voices heard. Yet many face violence, discrimination and other barriers when speaking out and putting forward their demands.

title: Sudan: Devastating RSF drone strikes on civilians in El Obeid should be investigated as war crimes
content:
Drone strikes by Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which hit residential areas and civilian infrastructure in El Obeid city, in Sudan’s North Kordofan State, killing dozens and disrupting essential services, should be investigated as war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization investigated nine RSF drone strikes in El Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026. Three of the strikes hit residential areas; four struck key civilian infrastructure, including El Obeid’s power plant, fuel stations, and the main market; and two targeted moving vehicles. In all incidents, interviewees said they either saw or heard the drones, moments before or after the strikes. Amnesty International’s investigation did not identify military objectives in the vicinity of the sites at the time they were struck.

title: Italy: “A bleak day for freedom of expression” as parliament votes through repressive definition of antisemitism into law
content:
Reacting to a vote by Italy’s parliament to formally adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Research, Policy, Advocacy and Campaigns, said: 

“Today marks a bleak day for freedom of expression as Italy explicitly makes the IHRA working definition of antisemitism legally binding. The new law, based on a definition that has long raised serious concerns because it conflates antisemitism with legitimate criticism of Israel, heightens the risk of far-reaching forms of censorship and self-censorship. Its application across schools, universities, social media platforms and beyond threatens a chilling effect and infringe on the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.

title: Türkiye: LGBTI rights defenders must be immediately released and charges against them dropped
content:
Ahead of the start of a hearing tomorrow in the case against the founders of the LGBTI organization Social Policy, Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation Studies Association (SPoD), the Human Rights Defenders Solidarity Network – a network of 38 organizations including Amnesty International Türkiye – have issued a joint statement. Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe, said: 

“It is deeply disturbing that four founding members of this organization, which has fought tirelessly against discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, are facing prison sentences for doing this vital work. These could be the first of many such prosecutions in the wake of a new LGBTI crackdown that threatens the existence of dozens of other organizations.

title: El Salvador: Public debt is mortgaging the country’s future without guaranteeing rights today
content:
The increase in public debt and indebtedness in El Salvador over the last decade has not led to a proportional and sustainable improvement in access to economic and social rights, according to Amnesty International’s new report, “When the budget does not guarantee rights”. 

The report analyses the evolution of the public budget between 2015 and 2025, documenting how the increasing debt burden, lack of transparency and a concentration of decision-making power within the executive branch have reduced the state’s capacity to mobilize the maximum of its available resources to uphold rights such as the right to health, to education and to social protection. 

“The findings highlight an alarming contradiction: the Salvadoran state is spending more and increasing its indebtedness, but these available resources do not manifest as equivalent improvements for the population. When debt servicing accounts for a larger proportion of the budget than health or education, it is legitimate to question where the money is going and why,” said Ana Piquer, Americas director at Amnesty International.

title: Azerbaijan: Abzas Media staff endure three years behind bars for independent journalism
content:
Ahead of the third anniversary of the earliest arrests of Abzas Media journalists in Azerbaijan, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:

“Three years on, seven Abzas Media journalists remain behind bars in desperate conditions, far from their families. They were among the first targets in what has become a sweeping crackdown on independent journalism in Azerbaijan.

“The reprisals do not end with unfounded imprisonment. Relatives and lawyers report increased use of solitary confinement, denial of health care, beatings and other ill-treatment against the Abzas Media journalists and others jailed for critical journalism and dissenting views.

“The Azerbaijani authorities must immediately and unconditionally release all those imprisoned solely for the exercise of their right to freedom of expression. They must provide all prisoners with adequate health care, promptly investigate reports of abuse and put an end to all forms of ill-treatment.”

title: Saudi Arabia/UN: Closure of ILO complaint a blow for migrant workers facing persistent abuse and discrimination
content:
Responding to the closure of the labour rights complaint filed against Saudi Arabia under Article 26 of the International Labour Organization (ILO) Constitution, following an agreement reached between Saudi Arabia and workers’ representative to the ILO, Iain Byrne, Amnesty International’s Head of Economic and Social Justice, said: 

“The premature closure of the formal complaint at the ILO against Saudi Arabia is a blow for the millions of migrant workers in the country.  

“The concerns that gave rise to the complaint remain unresolved. They include serious abuses linked to the persistence of the kafala system, which continues to leave migrant workers dependent on their employers and enables forced labour, exploitation and racial discrimination, while imposing substantial barriers to accessing justice.  

“While the agreement reached between the trade unions and the government sets out broad areas for future engagement, it fails to detail any specific legal or policy changes that Saudi Arabia has committed to undertake. It also fails so far to provide clear timelines for action, publicly available benchmarks or an independent monitoring mechanism.

title: Global: States’ failure to launch negotiations on an autonomous weapons treaty is a wasted opportunity
content:
Responding to news that states at the seventh Review Conference of High Contracting Parties to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) have failed to agree to negotiate a global treaty to address the growing threat posed by autonomous weapons systems, instead adopting a watered-down mandate for the development of an instrument with ambiguous legal status, Erika Guevara Rosas, Senior Director of Research Advocacy, Policy and Campaigns at Amnesty International said:

“Agreement to continue discussions for a further two years without a clear legal objective on the regulation of autonomous weapon systems (AWS) falls shamefully short of what is needed to meet the reality of the moment. If states are truly committed to tackling the risks of increasing autonomy in warfare, they must redouble their efforts to ensure that agreed norms are integrated into a robust, global legally binding treaty, probably outside the CCW. In addition to ensuring meaningful human control over the use of these weapons systems, states must also push for a ban on autonomous weapons systems that target humans.
